messages.content: You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A 2 Mb file crosses 3 links of 1 Mb/s as one unit. How long? With 10 packets of 0.2 Mb?
One unit: 3 × 2 = 6 s. Packets: (3+10−1) × 0.2 = 2.4 s. (See week-01.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why is hop-by-hop reliability not a substitute for an end-to-end check?
Faults can occur between the hop checks (router memory, software bugs, middleboxes) and the end application is the only party that knows what 'correct' means. (See week-01.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
What fraction of a 10 Gb/s Ethernet link carries TCP payload with 9000 B jumbo frames (IPv4)?
Payload 8960 B over 9000+38 = 9038 B on the wire: 99.1%. (See week-01.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does doubling link bandwidth not halve the latency of a 1 KB web request?
Transmission time is only part of delay; propagation, handshakes and queueing do not scale with bandwidth. (See week-01.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Minimum fibre RTT New York to London (5,570 km, route stretch 1.4, 2×10⁸ m/s)?
2 × 1.4 × 5570 / 200,000 = 78 ms. (See week-01.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A 100 Mb/s link with 10 ms one-way delay: BDP?
100×10⁶ × 0.02 / 8 = 250 KB. (See week-01.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A link serves 2000 pkt/s and receives 1800 pkt/s (M/M/1). Mean delay and mean queue length?
W = 1/(2000−1800) = 5 ms; L = 1800 × 0.005 = 9 packets. (See week-02.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does doubling a saturated link's capacity cut delay by far more than half?
W = 1/(μ−λ): at λ close to μ the denominator is tiny. Doubling μ greatly enlarges μ−λ, so delay can fall 10x or more. (See week-02.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Using P(queue > k) = ρᵏ⁺¹, how many buffer slots keep overflow below 1% at ρ = 0.8 (infinite-queue approximation)?
0.8^(k+1) < 0.01 → k+1 > ln0.01/ln0.8 = 20.6 → k = 20 slots. (See week-02.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A router has 10 Gb/s ports, 100 ms average RTT and 400 flows. What buffer does the BDP/√n rule give?
BDP = 125 MB; /√400 = 20 → 6.25 MB. (See week-02.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Show that the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula W = 1/μ + λE[S²]/(2(1−ρ)) reduces to M/M/1 for exponential service.
For exponential service E[S²] = 2/μ², so W = 1/μ + ρ/(μ(1−ρ)) = 1/(μ(1−ρ)) = 1/(μ−λ). For deterministic service E[S²] = 1/μ² halves the queueing term. (See week-02.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A server has 50 requests in the system on average and receives 200 requests/s. Mean response time?
Little: W = L/λ = 50/200 = 0.25 s. (See week-02.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does path-vector routing avoid count-to-infinity?
Each route carries its AS path; a router rejects any route whose path contains its own AS, so loops are detected immediately. (See week-03.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A stub AS has two providers. Why can it accidentally become a transit AS, and how is it prevented?
If it re-advertises one provider's routes to the other. Export filters (advertise only own and customer prefixes) prevent it. (See week-03.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A network has 100 links. At most how many LSA transmissions does one link-cost change trigger?
Each LSA crosses each link at most once per direction: ≤ 2E = 200. (See week-03.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does the MRAI timer slow convergence but protect routers?
It batches updates per neighbour (30 s), reducing churn and CPU load at the cost of delaying each propagation step, so path exploration takes longer in wall-clock time. (See week-03.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Path 100→200→300→400 where 100 is a customer of 200, 200 and 300 are peers, 400 is a customer of 300. Valley-free?
Yes: up (customer→provider), one peer link, then down (provider→customer). (See week-03.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why do split horizon and poisoned reverse not stop count-to-infinity in a loop of three routers?
They only prevent two-node loops; longer loops still circulate stale distances, so hold-down timers or path-vector routing are needed. (See week-03.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Reno average window if Wmax = 100 packets, RTT = 50 ms, MSS = 1460 B? Throughput?
Average ¾×100 = 75 packets. Throughput = 75×1460×8/0.05 ≈ 17.5 Mb/s. (See week-04.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why do AIAD controls fail to converge to fairness?
Both increase and decrease move parallel to the 45° line, so the difference x₁−x₂ never shrinks. (See week-04.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
How many RTTs does slow start with IW = 10 need to reach a window of 640?
10·2ⁿ ≥ 640 → n = 6 RTTs. (See week-04.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A Reno flow sees p = 10⁻⁴. What is W and average cwnd?
W = √(8/(3·10⁻⁴)) ≈ 163 packets; average ¾W ≈ 122 packets. (See week-04.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Jain's index J = (Σx)²/(n·Σx²) for rates (80, 10) and (45, 45)?
(90)²/(2·6500) = 0.62; and 1.0. (See week-04.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does Reno need a buffer of at least one BDP to keep a link busy?
After halving, the window is (BDP+B)/2, which must still be ≥ BDP, so B ≥ BDP. (See week-04.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why can a flow with 4x the RTT of another get only 1/4 of the throughput at equal loss?
Throughput ∝ 1/RTT: window growth is clocked by ACKs, so long-RTT flows grow slowly. (See week-05.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does BBR keep a minimum-RTT filter for 10 s and periodically reduce inflight?
To re-measure true propagation delay (RTprop) when queues are drained; otherwise standing queues would inflate the estimate. (See week-05.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
BtlBw = 50 Mb/s, RTprop = 80 ms. What is BBR's maximum inflight?
BDP = 500 KB; × cwnd_gain 2 = 1 MB (≈ 685 packets of 1460 B). (See week-05.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does CoDel use minimum sojourn time rather than average queue length?
A good queue (absorbing a burst) drains within an interval, so the minimum is low; a bad standing queue keeps even the minimum high. The average would confuse the two. (See week-05.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A 10 Mb/s uplink with a full 256 KB buffer: added queueing delay?
256,000 × 8 / 10⁷ = 0.205 s. (See week-05.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
How many bytes correspond to CoDel's 5 ms target on a 10 Mb/s link?
10⁷/8 × 0.005 = 6,250 bytes. (See week-05.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why can middleboxes block deployment of a new TCP option but not a new QUIC feature?
TCP headers are visible and parsed; QUIC encrypts nearly everything above UDP, leaving middleboxes nothing to drop selectively. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
What attack does 0-RTT enable and how do servers limit it?
Replay of early data. Servers restrict 0-RTT to idempotent requests and use anti-replay caches or single-use tickets. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
p = 0.5%, 40 packets in flight. P(at least one loss)?
1 − 0.995⁴⁰ = 1 − 0.818 = 18.2%. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does QUIC encrypt packet headers' transport fields?
To prevent middleboxes from depending on, or modifying, them: this keeps the protocol evolvable (anti-ossification) and hides metadata. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
SRTT = ⅞·SRTT + ⅛·R with SRTT = 100 ms and sample R = 180 ms. New SRTT?
87.5 + 22.5 = 110 ms. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
QUIC's server may send at most 3× the bytes it received before validating the client. A client Initial is padded to 1200 B. Server limit?
3600 bytes. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Decode the QUIC variable-length integer 0x7bbd and encode 37.
0x7bbd: top bits 01 → 2 bytes; clear them: 0x3bbd = 15,293. 37 < 64 → one byte 0x25. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Stream ID 6, 5 and 4: who initiated them and are they bidirectional?
6 = ...10 → client-initiated unidirectional; 5 = ...01 → server-initiated bidirectional; 4 = ...00 → client-initiated bidirectional. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
QUIC RTT estimator: first sample 120 ms, second sample 100 ms with ack delay 10 ms. smoothed RTT, rttvar and PTO (max_ack_delay 25 ms)?

First: srtt 120, var 60. Second: min = 100, 100 < 100 + 10 so no ack-delay adjustment; var = ¾·60 + ¼·|120−100| = 50; srtt = ⅞·120 + ⅛·100 = 117.5. PTO = 117.5 + 4·50 + 25 = 342.5 ms. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does the receive window cap a 100 ms path at about 5 Mb/s when it is 64 KB?
Throughput ≤ window/RTT = 65,536 × 8 / 0.1 s ≈ 5.2 Mb/s. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
At RTT 80 ms how much faster is the first byte with QUIC 1-RTT than with TCP+TLS 1.2?
TCP+TLS 1.2 needs 4 RTT = 320 ms; QUIC 1-RTT needs 2 RTT = 160 ms; it saves 160 ms. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why must the 'Initial' packet be padded to 1,200 bytes?

To bound amplification: the server may answer with at most 3× the bytes received before validating the client, so a larger client packet allows a useful server flight and a spoofed small request cannot cause large reflection. (See week-06.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why is full bisection bandwidth in a fat-tree not the same as no congestion?
It guarantees capacity only for ideal load balancing; ECMP hashing collisions and incast can still congest individual links. (See week-07.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
With α = 0.2 how much does DCTCP shrink cwnd, versus standard TCP?
DCTCP cuts by α/2 = 10 %; standard ECN-TCP halves (50 %). (See week-07.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A leaf has 32 × 25 Gb/s down and 8 × 100 Gb/s up. Oversubscription?
800/800 = 1:1 (non-blocking). (See week-07.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
How many hosts and switches does a k = 8 fat-tree have?
Hosts k³/4 = 128; switches 5k²/4 = 80. (See week-07.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
4 flows, 4 equal paths, ECMP: P(no collision)?
4!/4⁴ = 9.4%. (See week-07.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
DCTCP with α = 0.5: window cut?
α/2 = 25%. (See week-07.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Practice: a 100 ms RTT path with p = 10⁻⁶ and MSS 1460 B. Predict Reno throughput and compare with 10 Gb/s.
1.22×11680/0.1/0.001 ≈ 142 Mb/s: about 1.4% of the link; loss-based Reno cannot fill it. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Practice: Why can M/M/1 delay at 95% load be 10x that at 50% load?
W = 1/(μ−λ): (1−0.5)/(1−0.95) = 10. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A 1000 B packet crosses 5 hops at 10 Mb/s (store-and-forward, ignore propagation). End-to-end transmission delay?
5 × (8000/10⁷) = 4 ms. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A Reno flow halves cwnd from 120 to 60 after a loss. How many RTTs to recover?
Additive increase of 1 per RTT: 60 RTTs. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A fat-tree uses 8-port switches. Hosts and switches?
k³/4 = 128 hosts; 5k²/4 = 80 switches. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Which of TCP+TLS 1.3 and QUIC 1-RTT saves how much at RTT 80 ms?
3 RTT vs 2 RTT: saves 80 ms. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A 4 MB file crosses 4 store-and-forward links at 100 Mb/s using 1000 B packets (ignore propagation). Transfer time?
P = 4000 packets; T = (4 + 4000 − 1)·8000/10⁸ = 0.320 s. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
M/M/1, λ = 800, μ = 1000 pkt/s. Mean delay, mean number in system, and P(more than 10 packets in the system)?
W = 1/200 = 5 ms; L = 4; P(>10) = ρ¹¹ = 0.8¹¹ = 8.6%. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
x–y costs 3, y–z costs 4, x–z costs 9. What does distance-vector give for x's distance to z?
min(9, 3 + 4) = 7, via y. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A Reno flow halves its window from 200 to 100 at an RTT of 200 ms. Time to regain 200?
100 RTTs × 0.2 s = 20 s. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
RTT 120 ms. Time to first byte for TCP+TLS 1.3, QUIC 1-RTT and QUIC 0-RTT?
3 × 120 = 360 ms; 2 × 120 = 240 ms; 1 × 120 = 120 ms. (See week-08.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Choose CMS dimensions for ε = 0.001, δ = 0.01.
w = ⌈e/0.001⌉ = 2719, d = ⌈ln 100⌉ = 5, i.e. about 13,600 counters. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Name two drawbacks of a logically centralised controller.
Single point of failure/scalability and added control latency; mitigated by replicated, distributed controllers and proactive rule installation. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why are count-min sketches mergeable across switches?

With identical hash functions the counter arrays are linear: adding two sketches element-wise gives the sketch of the combined stream, so a controller can merge per-switch sketches. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
In a two-phase update, why must internal switches be updated before the ingress?
If ingress stamped the new version first, packets would reach internal switches lacking rules for it and be dropped. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Heavy hitters: flows > 1% of N = 10⁶ packets. A sketch with ε = 0.001 overestimates by at most how much?
εN = 1000 packets (w.h.p.), so a 10,000-packet threshold is reliable. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A ternary 5-tuple rule (104 bits) needs how many TCAM bits?
About 2 × 104 = 208 (two bits per ternary bit). (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A Bloom filter holds n = 1,000,000 items in 10 bits per item with k = 7 hash functions. Memory and false-positive rate?
m = 10⁷ bits = 1.25 MB; FPR ≈ (1 − e^(−0.7))⁷ = 0.5034⁷ ≈ 0.82%. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A reactive controller handles 10,000 new flows/s with 128-byte Packet-Ins. Control-channel bandwidth?
10,000 × 128 × 8 = 10.24 Mb/s (plus the Flow-Mods back), and every flow's first packet pays a controller round trip. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
2,000 hosts, exact-match all-pairs rules. Entries needed versus per-destination rules?
2,000 × 1,999 ≈ 4.0 million versus 2,000. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A ternary 5-tuple rule uses 104 key bits. How much TCAM do 1 million such rules need?
About 2 × 104 = 208 bits each → 208 Mbit ≈ 26 MB, far beyond typical TCAM capacities, so rules must be aggregated or kept in SRAM-based tables. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why must an incremental checksum update use the old and new 16-bit word?
The checksum is a one's-complement sum, so replacing a word m by m' changes it by (m' − m): HC' = ~(~HC + ~m + m'). (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why do the 10xxxxxx headers loop in the header-space lab?
Switch B sends them back to A, and A forwards all headers starting with 1 to B again. (See week-09.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Capacity of a 40 MHz channel at 30 dB?
40 × log₂(1001) ≈ 399 Mb/s. (See week-10.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why is RTS/CTS not enabled by default?
Its overhead exceeds the collision cost for small frames; it helps mainly with long frames and hidden terminals. (See week-10.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Compute FSPL at 5 GHz at 50 m.
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does doubling transmit power (+3 dB) give much less than 2x throughput at high SNR?
Capacity is logarithmic in SNR: +3 dB adds about one bit/s/Hz, so at 6.7 b/s/Hz that is a ~15% increase. (See week-10.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
One station at 1 Mb/s and one at 11 Mb/s each send 1500 B frames in turn (ignore overhead). Per-station throughput?
12 ms + 1.09 ms per round of two frames: 12,000 bits / 13.09 ms ≈ 0.92 Mb/s each. (See week-10.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why do 5 and 6 GHz networks need more access points than 2.4 GHz for equal coverage?
Free-space loss grows 6 dB per frequency doubling, and walls attenuate higher frequencies more. (See week-10.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does anycast not guarantee the closest server in latency terms?
BGP picks by policy and AS-path length, not distance or load, so a user may reach a distant site. (See week-11.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
In ABR, why is a conservative throughput estimate (e.g. harmonic mean) preferred to the arithmetic mean?
Outliers of high throughput inflate the arithmetic mean and cause stalls; the harmonic mean is dominated by low values. (See week-11.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
With an 8 s buffer, 3 Mb/s throughput and fixed 5 Mb/s chunks of 4 s, during which chunk download does the first stall occur?
Download takes 6.67 s. Chunk 1: buffer 8 → 1.33, +4 = 5.33 s. Chunk 2 needs 6.67 s > 5.33 s, so it stalls (1.33 s) during the second chunk. (See week-11.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
With 20 servers on a consistent-hash ring, what fraction of keys moves when one server is added?
About 1/21 ≈ 4.8%. (See week-11.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Harmonic versus arithmetic mean of 4, 4, 4 and 1 Mb/s?
Harmonic 4/1.75 = 2.29; arithmetic 3.25: the harmonic mean is the safer estimate. (See week-11.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A CDN has a 90% hit ratio and the origin can serve 10 Gb/s. Maximum total delivery rate?
10/(1−0.9) = 100 Gb/s. (See week-11.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A DNS server returns a 3,000 B reply to a 60 B query. Amplification factor?
3000/60 = 50x. (See week-12.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why does RPKI not stop all hijacks?
It validates only the origin AS; an attacker can forge the path and still appear to originate through the legitimate AS. (See week-12.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A server has a 4096-entry SYN backlog and 63 s half-open lifetime. SYN rate needed to fill it?
4096/63 ≈ 65 SYN/s. (See week-12.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A ROA authorises AS 64500 for 192.0.2.0/24, maxLength 24. What is the status of 192.0.2.0/25 from AS 64500?
Invalid: it is more specific than the maxLength allows. (See week-12.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A ROA covers 10.0.0.0/20 with maxLength 22 for AS 64500. Announcement 10.0.0.0/21 from AS 64500?
Valid: length 21 ≤ 22 and origin matches. (See week-12.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A 1 Tb/s attack is spread evenly over 10 anycast sites. Per-site load?
100 Gb/s (in the idealised case). (See week-12.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
At what distance does LEO beat fibre in the model above?
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why can a crowd-sourced speed test under-report a path's capacity?
It often measures the home Wi-Fi/access link, server load, or a single TCP flow limited by loss and RTT. (See week-13.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A Starlink-like shell at 1200 km altitude: orbital period?
a = 7571 km; T = 2π√(7571³/398600) ≈ 6,560 s ≈ 109 min. (See week-13.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
100 RTT samples have s = 15 ms. 95% CI half-width for the mean?
1.96 × 15/10 = 2.9 ms. (See week-13.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
With fibre stretch 1.2, at what distance does the LEO model beat fibre?
0.012d = 0.00733d + 7.33 → d ≈ 1,570 km. (See week-13.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why are medians and percentiles preferred to means for RTT?
RTT distributions are heavy-tailed; a few huge values distort the mean while percentiles describe typical and worst-case behaviour. (See week-13.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Ring all-reduce, N = 8 GPUs, S = 1 GB, B = 100 GB/s, ignore latency. Time?
2·(7/8)·1/100 s = 17.5 ms. (See week-14.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
Why is halving-doubling better than ring for small messages but not for large ones?
Both have the same bandwidth term; halving-doubling has 2·log₂N latency steps instead of 2(N−1), which only matters when latency dominates. (See week-14.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
A job's 16 GPUs use 4 equal-cost paths with 4 elephant flows. P(no collision)?
4!/4⁴ = 24/256 = 9.4%. (See week-14.html#exercises)
You are the teaching assistant for an Advanced Computer Networks course. Answer accurately and concisely.
RoCEv2 with 1,024-byte payloads: wire efficiency?
